title: US Envoy Sergio Gor: India Relationship Stronger Than Five Years Ago
excerpt: In an interview with India Today, US Ambassador Sergio Gor argues the strategic partnership has deepened across trade, defence and technology — and says the interim trade deal is effectively done.
body:
• US Ambassador Sergio Gor told India Today the US-India relationship "is stronger than it was five years ago," citing deeper cooperation on trade, defence and technology.
  • He said the interim trade agreement is effectively done — tariffs cut from 50% to 18% — with formal signing expected "very soon."
  • Gor stressed Washington's H-1B review is a broad immigration overhaul, not a measure targeting India.
  • He confirmed India has been invited to join Pax Silica, the US-led silicon supply chain initiative.

In an interview published in India Today's September 21 issue, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor told the magazine that the US relationship with India "is stronger than it was five years ago," pointing to expanded cooperation across trade, defence, critical technologies and supply chains.

The remarks come as the two governments work to close out a bilateral trade agreement that has dominated the bilateral agenda for more than a year. Gor, sworn in last November, said the interim trade deal is effectively complete, with only minor points left to settle.

Context & Background

Sergio Gor — born Sergey Gorokhovsky — is a longtime Donald Trump confidant who previously directed the White House Presidential Personnel Office. Confirmed by the Senate in October as part of a bloc of 107 nominees and sworn in that November, he arrived in New Delhi in early January as US Ambassador to India and Special Envoy for South and Central Asian affairs.

The trade dispute he inherited was substantial. Last August, Indian exporters faced 50% US tariffs — a 25% reciprocal levy plus a 25% punitive tariff tied to India's purchases of Russian oil. In early February, Trump announced the conclusion of the first tranche of interim trade agreement talks, rolling reciprocal tariffs back to 18% and eliminating the Russia-oil surcharge — claiming New Delhi had agreed to halt crude purchases from Moscow, a claim India has neither confirmed nor denied.

Gor credited the breakthrough to the leaders' personal chemistry. "All credit goes to President Trump and PM Modi," he told CNN News18 in February. "Since I arrived in India about a month ago, I have said that the two leaders have a great personal relationship and that is something that carried this deal forward."

"As I have said many times, President Trump genuinely considers Prime Minister Modi a great friend! Thrilled by the news of the trade deal this evening. The relationship between the United States and India has LIMITLESS POTENTIAL!"

— Sergio Gor, US Ambassador to India

Impact & Analysis

For businesses on both sides, Gor's "signing very soon" message is the practical signal. Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has said the interim trade agreement would likely be operationalised in April, while Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agarwal indicated an Indian delegation would visit the US to convert the joint understanding into legally binding language.

The legal mechanics remain complicated. After the US Supreme Court struck down the reciprocal tariffs, Washington applied a 10% auxiliary duty on all incoming goods under Section 122 of the Trade Act for a 150-day window beginning February 24, and launched Section 301 investigations into certain trading partners' industrial and labour practices. India has formally submitted responses, and consultations continue.

Beyond tariffs, Gor cited the widening commercial relationship: multi-billion-dollar technology investments in India from Amazon, Microsoft and Google; American CEOs visiting the US Embassy weekly to discuss relocating operations to India; and India's invitation to join Pax Silica, the US-led silicon supply chain initiative already joined by Japan, South Korea, the UK and Israel.

Diaspora Angle

Addressing anxiety among Indian professionals, he said the administration's review is part of a broader overhaul of US immigration — not aimed at Indian workers — and that curbing illegal immigration aligns with India's own position on illegal migration.

"The reality is there are tens of thousands of points. We're not dealing with a small country. This is one of the biggest economies. And so, we're thrilled that the interim deal is done. We have a few tweaking points left to address, but it's done. So, the signing will happen soon."

— Sergio Gor, US Ambassador to India

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals on H-1B visas — a community that watches every immigration policy shift closely — the framing of the review as systemic rather than India-specific offers some reassurance.

What's Next

The immediate milestone is the formal signing of the interim trade agreement and its operationalisation, expected by April, with negotiators also set to begin a second tranche covering a bilateral investment treaty, digital trade rules and intellectual property protections.

Gor himself suggested the trajectory is still upward: he has said he hopes Trump will visit India in the next year or two, and that no partner is more essential to the US than India.
